This supplement is a reference to use with units, rather than a demand to memorize every digit. c ≈ 3×1010 cm/s, G ≈ 6.7×10−8 cm³ g−1 s−2 1 pc ≈ 3×1018 cm, M☉ ≈ 2×1033 g h ≈ 6.6×10−27 erg s, me ≈ 9.1×10−28 g mec² ≈ 511 keV, α ≈ 1137 The reference values use CODATA 2022 and IAU definitions or nominal conversions, with measurement uncertainties omitted. Convert from SI metres, kilograms, and seconds by tracking each dimensional power. The SI value c = 299792458 m/s is exact; since 1 m = 100 cm, its CGS numerical value is one hundred times larger. 1 erg = 1 g cm² s−2 = 10−7 J 1 dyn = 1 g cm s−2 = 10−5 N 1 g/cm³ = 10³ kg/m³ 1 dyn/cm² = 0.1 Pa, 1 erg/cm³ = 0.1 J/m³ From F = Gm₁m₂/r², G has dimensions length³/(mass × time²). Going from SI to CGS multiplies its numerical value by 100³/1000 = 1000. G ≈ 6.67430×10−11 m³kg s² = 6.67430×10−8 cm³g s² Unlike c or h, G is measured. Its CODATA 2022 relative standard uncertainty is about 2.2×10⁻⁵. A long numerical value is not the same thing as an exact defining value. 03Connect parsecs, light-years, and solar masses The parsec originated with annual parallax and is defined as 1 pc = (648000/π) au. Since one arcsecond is π/648000 radians, this connects to the small-angle relation d ≈ 1 au/p. One au is exactly 149597870700 m. 1 pc ≈ 3.08568×1018 cm ≈ 3.26156 ly 1 kpc = 10³ pc, 1 Mpc = 10⁶ pc 1 ly = c×(365.25×86400 s) ≈ 9.46073×1017 cm The light-year here uses the Julian year of 365.25 days. The solar mass scale, about 2×10³³ g, is useful but is not an exact universal constant in kilograms. Orbital dynamics constrains GM well, and the IAU defines a nominal solar mass parameter. (GM)☉N = 1.3271244×1020 m³ s−2 (GM)☉NG ≈ 1.9884×1030 kg The superscript N denotes a nominal value. Nominal GM is an exact conversion reference, not a claim about the Sun’s instantaneous true GM. Dividing it by measured G introduces G’s uncertainty. 04h versus ℏ, and electron mass versus energy Frequency ν counts cycles per second, while angular frequency ω = 2πν measures phase change per second. Photon energy is hν = ℏω: the same physics with matching frequency conventions. ℏ = h2π, E = hν = ℏω = hcλ hc ≈ 1239.84 eV nm, ℏc ≈ 197.327 MeV fm Electron rest mass is me. The value 511 keV is the rest energy mec²; the mass can be written as 511 keV/c². An electron volt is an energy unit, not a voltage. 1 eV = 1.602176634×10−19 J = 1.602176634×10−12 erg mec² ≈ 8.18711×10−7 erg ≈ 0.510999 MeV The fine-structure constant α is dimensionless and has the same value in SI and Gaussian units. Its vacuum, low-energy value is approximately 1/137. It is distinct from the alpha used for disk transport efficiency. α = eSI²4πε₀ℏc = eG²ℏc ≈ 1137.036 12α²mec² ≈ 13.6 eV The final expression estimates the hydrogen ground-state binding energy with a fixed nucleus. Electron rest energy and α thus connect to atomic photon-energy scales. 05Unpack the Hubble constant’s units H₀ is the present expansion rate inferred from measurements and modelling, not an exact defining universal constant. Use 70 km/s/Mpc as a conversion example, not as a unique answer or a claim of current consensus. H₀ = 70×10⁵ cm/s3.08568×10²⁴ cm ≈ 2.2685×10−18 s−1 H₀−1 ≈ 4.408×1017 s ≈ 13.97 Gyr H₀⁻¹ is the Hubble time, not necessarily the age of the universe. The age depends on a cosmological model and the history of H(t). The dimensionless h in H₀ = 100h km/s/Mpc is also unrelated to Planck’s constant h. 06In Gaussian CGS, convert equations as well as values Electromagnetic CGS conventions include electrostatic, electromagnetic, and Gaussian systems. Here use Gaussian CGS explicitly: charge in statC and magnetic flux density B in gauss (G). Distinguish G as a magnetic unit from G as the gravitational constant. The same physics in matched conventions Quantity / lawSICGS–Gauss Coulomb-force magnitudeF = |q₁q₂|/(4πε₀r²)F = |q₁q₂|/r² Lorentz forceF⃗ = q(E⃗ + v⃗ × B⃗)F⃗ = q(E⃗ + (v⃗/c) × B⃗) Vacuum magnetic energy densityuB = B²/(2μ₀)uB = B²/(8π) Nonrelativistic electron gyrofrequencyωB = eB/mₑωB = eB/(mₑc) Classical electron radiusrₑ = e²/(4πε₀mₑc²)rₑ = e²/(mₑc²) Gaussian Coulomb’s law gives [q]² = [force][length]² = g cm³ s⁻², so charge has dimensions g1/2 cm3/2 s⁻¹. Electric and magnetic fields both have dimensions g1/2 cm−1/2 s⁻¹; v/c in the Lorentz force is dimensionless. 1 G = 10−4 T, 1 μG = 10−10 T 1 statC ≈ 3.33564×10−10 C Match charge and field values together with the equation’s coefficients. Do not insert SI charge numbers into Gaussian equations or simply set ε₀ and μ₀ to one. In the current SI, μ₀ is measured; μ₀ ≈ 4π×10⁻⁷ H/m is an approximation. For B = 1 G, Gaussian uB = 1/(8π) ≈ 0.03979 erg/cm³. Using 10⁻⁴ T in the SI formula gives about 0.003979 J/m³, agreeing after energy-density conversion. 07Try the conversions The field conversion also compares magnetic energy densities. An eV-to-K readout is the equivalent temperature from E = kBT, not an assignment of temperature to every possible particle population. CHECK THE UNITS Calculate with the units When converting 1 pc from metres to centimetres, and electron mass from kilograms to grams, what are the factors? Why is the factor for G not one hundred? Show the answer Length gains a factor 100 and mass a factor 1000. Since G has dimensions length³/mass/time², its factor is 100³/1000 = 1000. Writing dimensions first helps prevent exponent mistakes. REFERENCES & NUMERICAL SOURCES Fundamental values use CODATA 2022. Unit conventions follow NRAO; definitions and nominal scales follow IAU. H₀ = 70 is illustrative.
